title: Narada and the water of maya
hookLine: Narada asks to see maya and loses a lifetime fetching a cup of water
carry: maya: the one appearing as many, or god's power
tomorrow: which Sanskrit words name seeing, hearing, breathing?

cards: The sage Narada once asked to be shown maya. In an old story, as Swami Vivekananda told it in a lecture, Krishna says: first, fetch me some water. Narada goes to a village, and a young woman opens the door.
He forgets the water. He marries her, farms, raises children; years pass. Then a flood comes, and the river takes the house, the wife, the children.
Narada sits on the bank, weeping. And a voice behind him says: where's my water? I've been waiting nearly half an hour.

teach.b: In the Gita, Krishna names the same thing: daivi hy esha gunamayi mama maya duratyaya. This divine maya of mine, made of the gunas, is hard to cross. Then: mam eva ye prapadyante mayam etam taranti te.
Those who come to me cross over it. So what is maya? It's one of Hinduism's great teachings, and two classic schools read it two ways.

teach.h: ADVAITA: THE ONE APPEARING AS MANY.
teach.b: In Advaita, linked with Shankara, there is one reality, Brahman, and maya is how that one appears as many. Narada's years weren't nothing; they were real enough to weep over, the way a dream is real while it lasts.
But they weren't the final truth, and crossing maya means waking to the one.

In Vishishtadvaita, linked with Ramanuja, maya in this verse is God's own wondrous power, the stuff of the world he works through. The world is real, and it belongs to God the way a body belongs to a self.
Crossing maya means not being swallowed by it, by turning to the one who wields it.
Each side at its strongest. Advaita: if there's truly one, the many must be a kind of appearance. Ramanuja: if God calls the power his own, calling the world unreal sells his work short.
And notice what both share, and what Narada learned by the river: maya belongs to God, it can catch anyone, even a sage, and the way across is to turn back toward God.

how: Hindu teachers in the Advaita and Vishishtadvaita lines still teach the Gita with their school's classic commentary, and students often read Gita 7.14 with more than one commentary side by side.

games.q: who reads it how — tap the pairs.
p: maya as God's real, wondrous power

s: every Hindu school reads maya as illusion
Advaita reads it as appearance; Ramanuja's school reads it as God's real power.
in Gita 7.14 Krishna calls it mama maya, my maya
and says it is hard to cross; those who come to him cross over it.
in the story, Narada learns about maya from a lecture
he lives it: a whole life, a flood, and then Krishna asking, where's my water?

games.q: your friend loves Ramanuja's reading and asks you to give Advaita's best case in one line. which do you send?
o: 'if there's truly one reality, the many must be how it appears.'
'the world is fake, so nothing you do matters.'
'maya is God's real power, and the world is his.'
games.why: that's Advaita at its strongest: one reality, appearing as many. the second is a caricature; the third is Ramanuja's own view.

practice: Pick one object near you, a cup, a leaf, your own hand, and look at it for the sit. For a while, see it as Advaita might: a form the one reality is wearing. Then as Ramanuja might: something real, shaped and held.

wordCard.voice: Two hundred core words: today, maya, and mama, mine. One verse, two classic readings: the one appearing as many, or God's own wondrous power. Either way, it's his.

orig.note: Sanskrit: maya; in Gita 7.14 it is Krishna's own, mama maya, and hard to cross.

carryVoice: Keep this one: maya, the one appearing as many, or God's own power. Either way it belongs to God, and it can be crossed.
